--- title: "Data Visualization for Data Scientists: From Question to Plot" description: "A practical, Python-first guide to common Data Science plots with simulated data, reproducible code and interactive examples." author: "MLStation" date: 2026-10-02 categories: [Data Science, Visualization, Python] draft: false ---
📊 A good plot is not decoration. It is a question made visible.
Choose the **question first**, the **plot second**, and the **library third**.
Every worked example follows one contract:
QUESTION → DATA SIMULATOR → PLOT CODE → VISIBLE CHART → INTERPRETATION
The chart is always visible. **View Data Simulator** and **View Plot Code** expand and collapse independently. This lets a beginner focus on the picture first and inspect reproducible Python when ready. ::: {.callout-tip} ## What you will learn Distribution, comparison, relationship, time-series, experimentation, multivariate, model-diagnostic, geographic and interactive visualization using Matplotlib, Seaborn, Plotly and Bokeh, plus guidance on modern alternatives. ::: # 1. Visualization Starts with the Question
🔍 Distribution
Histogram · KDE · ECDF · Box · Violin
⚖️ Comparison
Bar · Box · Error bars · Small multiples
🔗 Relationship
Scatter · Regression · Hexbin
⏱️ Time
Line · Rolling trend · Uncertainty band
🤖 Model
Confusion · ROC · PR · Calibration · Residuals
🌍 Location / Flow
Maps · Funnels
# 2. The Python Visualization Ecosystem **Matplotlib** is the low-level foundation and is commonly static-first. **Seaborn** builds statistical graphics on Matplotlib. **Plotly** and **Bokeh** make browser interaction—hover, zoom, selection and widgets—a central strength. Matplotlib can also use interactive backends, so “Matplotlib is never interactive” is not technically correct. ## 2.1. Matplotlib — Precise Figure Control **Company question:** How is weekly revenue changing? ::: {#d9086186 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(1) mat_df=pd.DataFrame({"week":np.arange(1,21)}) mat_df["revenue"]=85000+1800*mat_df["week"]+rng.normal(0,4500,20) ``` ::: ::: {#ec815475 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)) ax.plot(mat_df["week"],mat_df["revenue"],marker="o") ax.set(title="Weekly Revenue",xlabel="Week",ylabel="Revenue ($)") fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-3-output-1.png){width=1264 height=623} ::: ::: **Best for:** custom static analytical figures, reports, annotations and fine control. ## 2.2. Seaborn — Statistical Visualization **Company question:** How does revenue differ across segments? ::: {#22680d1c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(2) seg=rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],900,p=[.55,.3,.15]) base=pd.Series(seg).map({"Consumer":70,"SMB":125,"Enterprise":220}).to_numpy() sns_df=pd.DataFrame({"segment":seg,"revenue":np.maximum(5,base+rng.normal(0,32,900))}) ``` ::: ::: {#563b0b63 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,4)) sns.boxplot(data=sns_df,x="segment",y="revenue",ax=ax) ax.set(title="Monthly Revenue by Segment",ylabel="Revenue ($)") fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=1184 height=623} ::: ::: **Best for:** EDA, grouped distributions, statistical comparisons and regression views. ## 2.3. Plotly — Interactive Exploration **Company question:** Which individual customers sit behind the overall pattern? ::: {#7caddfdd .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(3); n=650 px_df=pd.DataFrame({"customer_id":np.arange(10001,10001+n),"segment":rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],n,p=[.55,.3,.15]),"sessions":rng.poisson(9,n)+1,"tickets":rng.poisson(1.5,n)}) px_df["revenue"]=25+5.5*px_df["sessions"]+px_df["segment"].map({"Consumer":0,"SMB":40,"Enterprise":110})+rng.normal(0,25,n) ``` ::: ::: {#5aa5d9b9 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig=px.scatter(px_df,x="sessions",y="revenue",color="segment",size="tickets",hover_data=["customer_id"],title="Interactive Customer Explorer") fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Hover, zoom, pan, select and toggle legend groups directly in the rendered chart. ## 2.4. Bokeh — Interactive Browser Plots **Company question:** Can an analyst inspect and zoom into customers? ::: {#2a843281 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(4); n=500 bk_df=pd.DataFrame({"customer_id":np.arange(1,n+1),"sessions":rng.poisson(10,n)+1}) bk_df["revenue"]=(35+6*bk_df["sessions"]+rng.normal(0,30,n)).clip(5) ``` ::: ::: {#c566bbbe .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} from bokeh.plotting import figure,show from bokeh.models import ColumnDataSource,HoverTool source=ColumnDataSource(bk_df) p=figure(width=800,height=380,title="Bokeh: Revenue vs Sessions",tools="pan,wheel_zoom,box_zoom,reset") p.scatter(x="sessions",y="revenue",source=source,size=7,alpha=.45) p.add_tools(HoverTool(tooltips=[("Customer","@customer_id"),("Revenue","@revenue{0.0}")])) show(p) ``` ::: Bokeh is especially useful for linked selections, widgets and browser applications. # 3. Histogram — Distribution Shape **Company question:** What does monthly customer revenue look like? ::: {#d8f4a254 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(10) hist_df=pd.DataFrame({"revenue":rng.lognormal(4.35,.62,2500)}) ``` ::: ::: {#f7edce6f .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); ax.hist(hist_df["revenue"],bins=38,edgecolor="white") ax.set(title="Distribution of Monthly Revenue",xlabel="Revenue ($)",ylabel="Customers"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=1262 height=623} ::: :::
Bin width matters. Too few bins hide structure; too many emphasize noise.
# 4. KDE — Smooth Distribution Comparison **Company question:** Do segments have differently shaped revenue distributions? ::: {#5fa8fcfb .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(11) kde_df=pd.concat([pd.DataFrame({"segment":s,"revenue":rng.lognormal(mu,sd,700)}) for s,mu,sd in [("Consumer",4,.55),("SMB",4.55,.48),("Enterprise",5.25,.40)]],ignore_index=True) ``` ::: ::: {#ecdcc034 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); sns.kdeplot(data=kde_df,x="revenue",hue="segment",common_norm=False,ax=ax) ax.set(title="Revenue Density by Segment",xlabel="Revenue ($)"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=1264 height=623} ::: ::: KDE is estimated smoothness. Do not interpret every bump as a real population mode. # 5. ECDF — Cumulative Distribution **Company question:** What fraction of each segment falls below a revenue threshold? ::: {#104be821 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(12) ecdf_df=pd.concat([pd.DataFrame({"segment":s,"revenue":np.maximum(5,rng.normal(c,c*.28,600))}) for s,c in [("Consumer",65),("SMB",125),("Enterprise",225)]],ignore_index=True) ``` ::: ::: {#d3eb1e4e .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); sns.ecdfplot(data=ecdf_df,x="revenue",hue="segment",ax=ax) ax.set(title="ECDF of Revenue by Segment",xlabel="Revenue ($)",ylabel="Fraction ≤ x"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=1264 height=623} ::: ::: The ECDF has no histogram-bin choice and makes percentile questions direct. # 6. Box Plot — Compact Group Comparison **Company question:** Which segment has the widest revenue distribution? ::: {#dba8b9a5 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(13) box_df=pd.DataFrame({"segment":np.repeat(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],500)}) c=box_df["segment"].map({"Consumer":70,"SMB":130,"Enterprise":230}).to_numpy(); box_df["revenue"]=np.maximum(5,c+rng.normal(0,c*.25)) ``` ::: ::: {#7dbdfd45 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5,4)); sns.boxplot(data=box_df,x="segment",y="revenue",ax=ax) ax.set(title="Revenue by Segment",ylabel="Revenue ($)"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-17-output-1.png){width=1184 height=623} ::: ::: Box plots summarize median, quartiles, spread and potential outliers. # 7. Violin + Strip — Shape and Observations **Company question:** Do plans differ in the whole engagement distribution? ::: {#a904dce9 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(14) violin_df=pd.DataFrame({"plan":np.repeat(["Standard","Premium"],220),"engagement":np.r_[rng.beta(2.2,4,220),rng.beta(4,2.4,220)]}) ``` ::: ::: {#ec08bddf .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); sns.violinplot(data=violin_df,x="plan",y="engagement",inner=None,ax=ax); sns.stripplot(data=violin_df,x="plan",y="engagement",alpha=.28,size=2.5,ax=ax) ax.set_title("Engagement Distribution by Plan"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-19-output-1.png){width=1104 height=623} ::: ::: Use violin plots when distribution shape itself matters. # 8. Bar Plot — Categorical Summary **Company question:** Which segment has the highest churn rate? ::: {#1a628cca .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(15); n=2400 seg=rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],n,p=[.55,.3,.15]); prob=pd.Series(seg).map({"Consumer":.19,"SMB":.13,"Enterprise":.08}).to_numpy(); raw=pd.DataFrame({"segment":seg,"churn":rng.binomial(1,prob)}); bar_df=raw.groupby("segment",as_index=False).agg(churn_rate=("churn","mean")) ``` ::: ::: {#a2f1bdd5 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.bar(bar_df["segment"],bar_df["churn_rate"]); ax.set(title="Churn Rate by Segment",ylabel="Churn rate",ylim=(0,bar_df["churn_rate"].max()*1.25)); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-21-output-1.png){width=1104 height=623} ::: :::
Bar lengths need an honest baseline. Truncating the y-axis can exaggerate differences.
# 9. Count Plot — Group Size **Company question:** How many customers use each device? ::: {#b99dbc8b .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(16) count_df=pd.DataFrame({"device":rng.choice(["Web","iOS","Android"],1800,p=[.46,.28,.26]),"segment":rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],1800,p=[.56,.3,.14])}) ``` ::: ::: {#236be17f .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); sns.countplot(data=count_df,x="device",hue="segment",ax=ax); ax.set(title="Customer Count by Device and Segment",ylabel="Customers"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-23-output-1.png){width=1264 height=623} ::: ::: Inspect sample size before interpreting subgroup metrics. # 10. Scatter Plot — Numerical Relationship **Company question:** Do more sessions correspond to more revenue? ::: {#3b0ea98e .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(17); n=1300 scatter_df=pd.DataFrame({"sessions":rng.poisson(10,n)+1}); scatter_df["revenue"]=(30+6.2*scatter_df["sessions"]+rng.normal(0,32,n)).clip(5) ``` ::: ::: {#7e91e1eb .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4.5)); ax.scatter(scatter_df["sessions"],scatter_df["revenue"],alpha=.25,s=18); ax.set(title="Sessions vs Monthly Revenue",xlabel="Sessions",ylabel="Revenue ($)"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-25-output-1.png){width=1261 height=703} ::: ::: Look for direction, curvature, clusters, changing variance and outliers. # 11. Regression Plot — Average Trend **Company question:** What average relationship is visible? ::: {#bf5e918e .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(18); n=900 reg_df=pd.DataFrame({"sessions":rng.uniform(1,25,n)}); reg_df["revenue"]=25+5.8*reg_df["sessions"]+rng.normal(0,28,n) ``` ::: ::: {#5a79e3ab .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4.5)); sns.regplot(data=reg_df,x="sessions",y="revenue",scatter_kws={"alpha":.18,"s":18},ax=ax); ax.set_title("Average Revenue Trend with Sessions"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-27-output-1.png){width=1264 height=703} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning} A fitted trend summarizes association, not causation. ::: # 12. Hexbin — Dense Relationships **Company question:** How do two telemetry measures relate across 75,000 events? ::: {#e873e745 .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np rng=np.random.default_rng(19); n=75000 hex_x=rng.normal(size=n); hex_y=.65*hex_x+rng.normal(0,.75,n) ``` ::: ::: {#c51afa30 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,5)); hb=ax.hexbin(hex_x,hex_y,gridsize=45,mincnt=1); fig.colorbar(hb,ax=ax,label="Observations"); ax.set(title="Density Hidden by Overplotting",xlabel="Feature X",ylabel="Feature Y"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-29-output-1.png){width=1077 height=783} ::: ::: Use hexbin, density, sampling or rasterization when scatter points become an opaque cloud. # 13. Line Plot — Change Over Time **Company question:** Is revenue rising beneath daily noise? ::: {#1402dc45 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(20); dates=pd.date_range("2026-01-01",periods=220,freq="D"); t=np.arange(220) line_df=pd.DataFrame({"date":dates,"revenue":120000+180*t+10000*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/7)+rng.normal(0,6500,220)}); line_df["rolling_14d"]=line_df["revenue"].rolling(14).mean() ``` ::: ::: {#f5350d24 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(10,4)); ax.plot(line_df["date"],line_df["revenue"],alpha=.35,label="Daily"); ax.plot(line_df["date"],line_df["rolling_14d"],linewidth=2,label="14-day mean"); ax.set(title="Revenue: Noise vs Trend",ylabel="Revenue ($)"); ax.legend(); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-31-output-1.png){width=1584 height=623} ::: ::: Chronology is information. Keep time on an ordered axis. # 14. Uncertainty Band — Show What We Do Not Know **Company question:** Is a conversion trend larger than its uncertainty? ::: {#69d19709 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(21); w=np.arange(1,21); est=.12+.002*w+rng.normal(0,.004,20); se=np.linspace(.012,.006,20) band_df=pd.DataFrame({"week":w,"estimate":est,"lower":est-1.96*se,"upper":est+1.96*se}) ``` ::: ::: {#c4741fbe .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(8,4)); ax.plot(band_df["week"],band_df["estimate"],linewidth=2); ax.fill_between(band_df["week"],band_df["lower"],band_df["upper"],alpha=.2); ax.set(title="Conversion Estimate with 95% Band",xlabel="Week",ylabel="Conversion rate"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-33-output-1.png){width=1264 height=623} ::: ::: Use uncertainty bands for forecasts, experiments and estimated quantities. # 15. Error Bars — Experiment Estimates **Company question:** How do A/B variants compare with uncertainty? ::: {#8abb80ad .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd exp_df=pd.DataFrame({"variant":["Control","Treatment A","Treatment B"],"conversion":[.100,.112,.107],"n":[12000,11850,12120]}); exp_df["se"]=np.sqrt(exp_df["conversion"]*(1-exp_df["conversion"])/exp_df["n"]); exp_df["ci95"]=1.96*exp_df["se"] ``` ::: ::: {#a16c5896 .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.errorbar(exp_df["variant"],exp_df["conversion"],yerr=exp_df["ci95"],fmt="o",capsize=5); ax.set(title="Conversion ± 95% Approximate CI",ylabel="Conversion rate"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-35-output-1.png){width=1101 height=623} ::: ::: Effect magnitude and uncertainty belong in the same comparison. # 16. Correlation Heatmap — Matrix Pattern **Company question:** Which numerical variables move together? ::: {#5b2944c1 .cell execution_count=35} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(22); n=1200 heat_df=pd.DataFrame({"sessions":rng.poisson(10,n)+1,"tenure":rng.integers(1,72,n),"tickets":rng.poisson(1.5,n)}); heat_df["revenue"]=25+6*heat_df["sessions"]+.6*heat_df["tenure"]+rng.normal(0,30,n); heat_df["satisfaction"]=np.clip(4.5-.28*heat_df["tickets"]+rng.normal(0,.5,n),1,5); corr=heat_df.corr(numeric_only=True) ``` ::: ::: {#e3ad9fcc .cell execution_count=36} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,5)); sns.heatmap(corr,annot=True,fmt=".2f",center=0,ax=ax); ax.set_title("Correlation Matrix"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-37-output-1.png){width=1052 height=783} ::: ::: Correlation is a screening tool, not a causal map. # 17. Pair Plot — Multivariate First Look **Company question:** How do several customer measures relate at once? ::: {#4bdea3e3 .cell execution_count=37} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(23); n=450 pair_df=pd.DataFrame({"segment":rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],n,p=[.55,.3,.15]),"sessions":rng.poisson(9,n)+1,"tenure":rng.integers(1,72,n),"satisfaction":np.clip(rng.normal(4,.65,n),1,5)}); pair_df["revenue"]=30+5.5*pair_df["sessions"]+pair_df["segment"].map({"Consumer":0,"SMB":40,"Enterprise":105})+rng.normal(0,25,n) ``` ::: ::: {#33e9c29d .cell execution_count=38} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns g=sns.pairplot(pair_df,vars=["sessions","revenue","tenure","satisfaction"],hue="segment",corner=True); g.fig.suptitle("Multivariate Customer Overview",y=1.02); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-39-output-1.png){width=1786 height=1637} ::: ::: Pair plots are excellent for early EDA but become unwieldy as the number of variables grows. # 18. Faceting — Small Multiples **Company question:** Does a relationship change by segment? ::: {#033ad006 .cell execution_count=39} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(24); n=1000 facet_df=pd.DataFrame({"segment":rng.choice(["Consumer","SMB","Enterprise"],n,p=[.55,.3,.15]),"device":rng.choice(["Web","iOS","Android"],n),"sessions":rng.poisson(9,n)+1}); facet_df["revenue"]=25+5.8*facet_df["sessions"]+facet_df["segment"].map({"Consumer":0,"SMB":45,"Enterprise":110})+rng.normal(0,30,n) ``` ::: ::: {#10fa91c9 .cell execution_count=40} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns g=sns.relplot(data=facet_df,x="sessions",y="revenue",col="segment",hue="device",kind="scatter",alpha=.45,height=3.3); g.fig.suptitle("Sessions vs Revenue Across Segments",y=1.05); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-41-output-1.png){width=1734 height=562} ::: ::: Small multiples often beat one overloaded plot with too many visual encodings. # 19. Interactive Time Series — Zoom into Events **Company question:** Can an analyst inspect a long timeline around an incident? ::: {#ac5e68fa .cell execution_count=41} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(27); dates=pd.date_range("2025-01-01",periods=420,freq="D"); t=np.arange(420) its_df=pd.DataFrame({"date":dates,"revenue":100000+120*t+8000*np.sin(2*np.pi*t/7)+rng.normal(0,5500,420)}); its_df["rolling_21d"]=its_df["revenue"].rolling(21).mean() ``` ::: ::: {#f1fb7520 .cell execution_count=42} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig=px.line(its_df,x="date",y=["revenue","rolling_21d"],title="Interactive Revenue Timeline"); fig.update_xaxes(rangeslider_visible=True); fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The range slider and zoom controls are valuable for campaigns, incidents and long monitoring windows. # 20. Confusion Matrix — Classification Errors **Company question:** Is the churn model missing positives or generating false alarms? ::: {#f83c49f1 .cell execution_count=43} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np rng=np.random.default_rng(30); n=2500 cm_y=rng.binomial(1,.18,n); cm_score=np.clip(.12+.55*cm_y+rng.normal(0,.22,n),0,1); cm_pred=(cm_score>=.5).astype(int) ``` ::: ::: {#c59a2cf0 .cell execution_count=44} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix,ConfusionMatrixDisplay cm=confusion_matrix(cm_y,cm_pred); ConfusionMatrixDisplay(cm,display_labels=["No churn","Churn"]).plot(); plt.title("Churn Classifier: Confusion Matrix"); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-45-output-1.png){width=940 height=750} ::: ::: A confusion matrix shows *which kind* of error occurs, not merely how often the model is correct. # 21. ROC Curve — Ranking Across Thresholds **Company question:** How well does the classifier separate classes? ::: {#26a0ce80 .cell execution_count=45} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np rng=np.random.default_rng(31); n=2800 roc_y=rng.binomial(1,.20,n); roc_score=np.clip(.10+.60*roc_y+rng.normal(0,.24,n),0,1) ``` ::: ::: {#4dc73ff1 .cell execution_count=46} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve,roc_auc_score fpr,tpr,_=roc_curve(roc_y,roc_score); auc=roc_auc_score(roc_y,roc_score); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,5)); ax.plot(fpr,tpr,label=f"AUC={auc:.3f}"); ax.plot([0,1],[0,1],linestyle="--"); ax.set(title="ROC Curve",xlabel="False Positive Rate",ylabel="True Positive Rate"); ax.legend(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-47-output-1.png){width=796 height=750} ::: ::: ROC summarizes threshold-dependent ranking behavior. # 22. Precision–Recall Curve — Rare Positive Classes **Company question:** What tradeoff is available when positive cases are scarce? ::: {#af46ce65 .cell execution_count=47} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np rng=np.random.default_rng(32); n=3500 pr_y=rng.binomial(1,.08,n); pr_score=np.clip(.05+.58*pr_y+rng.normal(0,.23,n),0,1) ``` ::: ::: {#9a7aaee8 .cell execution_count=48} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve,average_precision_score p,r,_=precision_recall_curve(pr_y,pr_score); ap=average_precision_score(pr_y,pr_score); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,5)); ax.plot(r,p,label=f"AP={ap:.3f}"); ax.set(title="Precision–Recall Curve",xlabel="Recall",ylabel="Precision"); ax.legend(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-49-output-1.png){width=796 height=750} ::: ::: Often more operationally revealing than accuracy for rare events such as fraud. # 23. Calibration — Can We Trust 0.8? **Company question:** Do predicted probabilities correspond to observed frequencies? ::: {#93b6232f .cell execution_count=49} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np rng=np.random.default_rng(33); n=4500 x=rng.normal(size=n); true_p=1/(1+np.exp(-1.3*x)); cal_y=rng.binomial(1,true_p); cal_score=np.clip(1/(1+np.exp(-.75*x)),.001,.999) ``` ::: ::: {#659b59ec .cell execution_count=50} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from sklearn.calibration import calibration_curve obs,pred=calibration_curve(cal_y,cal_score,n_bins=10); fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5,5)); ax.plot(pred,obs,marker="o"); ax.plot([0,1],[0,1],linestyle="--"); ax.set(title="Calibration Plot",xlabel="Mean predicted probability",ylabel="Observed positive rate"); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-51-output-1.png){width=796 height=750} ::: ::: Ranking quality and probability calibration are different properties. # 24. Residual Plot — Regression Diagnostics **Company question:** Does prediction error change systematically? ::: {#692e94d1 .cell execution_count=51} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(34); n=1200 actual=rng.normal(100,25,n); predicted=actual+.10*(actual-100)+rng.normal(0,12,n); resid_df=pd.DataFrame({"predicted":predicted,"residual":actual-predicted}) ``` ::: ::: {#c302f2bd .cell execution_count=52} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4.5)); ax.scatter(resid_df["predicted"],resid_df["residual"],alpha=.28); ax.axhline(0,linestyle="--"); ax.set(title="Residual Plot",xlabel="Predicted",ylabel="Actual − Predicted"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-53-output-1.png){width=1104 height=703} ::: ::: Residuals can reveal bias, nonlinearity and changing variance hidden by a single RMSE. # 25. Feature Importance — What Does the Model Rely On? **Company question:** Which inputs contribute most under this importance definition? ::: {#9b5b1003 .cell execution_count=53} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import pandas as pd imp_df=pd.DataFrame({"feature":["last_login_days","support_tickets","tenure","monthly_spend","sessions"],"importance":[.31,.25,.19,.14,.11]}).sort_values("importance") ``` ::: ::: {#6a78f1c2 .cell execution_count=54} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(7,4)); ax.barh(imp_df["feature"],imp_df["importance"]); ax.set(title="Model Feature Importance",xlabel="Importance"); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](data-visualization-for-data-scientists_files/figure-html/cell-55-output-1.png){width=1104 height=623} ::: :::
Importance is not causality. A predictive feature can be a proxy, consequence, correlated signal or leakage.
# 26. Funnel — Where Do Users Drop Out? **Company question:** At which purchase stage is the largest loss? ::: {#7f469156 .cell execution_count=55} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import pandas as pd funnel_df=pd.DataFrame({"stage":["Visitors","Product View","Cart","Checkout","Purchase"],"users":[100000,62000,21000,12000,9200]}) ``` ::: ::: {#1368b753 .cell execution_count=56} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig=px.funnel(funnel_df,x="users",y="stage",title="Purchase Funnel"); fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Common in acquisition, onboarding, checkout and application workflows. # 27. Geographic Plot — When Location Matters **Company question:** Where are orders concentrated around a service area? ::: {#1a41881d .cell execution_count=57} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Data Simulator"} import numpy as np import pandas as pd rng=np.random.default_rng(35); n=500 geo_df=pd.DataFrame({"latitude":30.27+rng.normal(0,.055,n),"longitude":-97.74+rng.normal(0,.065,n),"orders":rng.poisson(5,n)+1}) ``` ::: ::: {#e1c4453e .cell execution_count=58} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="View Plot Code"} import plotly.express as px fig=px.scatter_map(geo_df,lat="latitude",lon="longitude",size="orders",hover_data=["orders"],zoom=9,height=500,center={"lat": 30.2672, "lon": -97.7431},title="Interactive Geographic Distribution of Orders"); fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: Use a map when spatial relationships matter. If the question is only “which region is largest?”, a sorted bar chart may be clearer. # 28. Other Modern Visualization Libraries - **Altair** — declarative grammar-of-graphics and concise interactive statistical charts. - **hvPlot / HoloViews** — high-level interactive plotting for DataFrame/xarray workflows. - **Datashader** — rasterizes/aggregates huge datasets rather than drawing every point. - **PyDeck / deck.gl ecosystem** — rich large-scale geospatial visualization.
The state of the art is not “use the newest library.” Match the tool to data volume + analytical question + audience + interaction + deployment environment.
# 29. Which Library Should I Reach For? | Need | Good starting choice | |---|---| | Custom static figure | Matplotlib | | Statistical EDA | Seaborn | | Publication/report control | Matplotlib | | Interactive exploration | Plotly | | Browser widgets / linked interaction | Bokeh | | Declarative grammar | Altair | | Huge point clouds | Datashader ecosystem | | Interactive geospatial work | Plotly / PyDeck | # 30. Visualization Mistakes That Mislead - **Truncated bar axes** can exaggerate small differences. - **Too many categories** turn legends into puzzles. - **Dual y-axes** can manufacture apparent relationships through scaling. - **Many-slice pie charts** make precise comparison difficult. - **Rainbow scales** can create false perceptual boundaries. - **Lines between unrelated categories** imply continuity that does not exist. - **Means without uncertainty/sample size** can hide noise. - **Overplotting** calls for transparency, sampling, hexbin, density or rasterization. # 31. Exploratory vs Explanatory Visualization **Exploratory:** “What is happening?” → many views, interaction, diagnostics. **Explanatory:** “Here is what matters.” → fewer views, intentional ordering, annotation, uncertainty, restrained color.
EDA → DISCOVERY → ANALYSIS → DECISION → COMMUNICATION
# 32. A Data Scientist's Plot Selector ```text ONE NUMERIC → Histogram / KDE / ECDF / Box NUMERIC + CATEGORY → Box / Violin / Bar + CI TWO NUMERIC → Scatter / Regression / Hexbin TIME → Line / Rolling trend / Uncertainty band MATRIX → Heatmap CLASSIFIER → Confusion / ROC / PR / Calibration REGRESSION → Actual-vs-predicted / Residuals LOCATION → Map only when spatial structure matters ``` # 33. A Company Visualization Workflow If Product asks **“Why did conversion fall last month?”**: 1. Line plot → *when did it begin?* 2. Facets → *which device/segment/region?* 3. Funnel → *which stage?* 4. Distributions → *did population mix change?* 5. Event annotations → *what changed around that date?* 6. Statistical analysis → *is the change beyond noise?* 7. Explanatory chart → *communicate the finding.* # 34. The Visualization Ladder
SEE → COMPARE → RELATE → SEGMENT → DIAGNOSE → EXPLORE → EXPLAIN → SHIP
# 35. Final Perspective
✨ Choose the question first. Choose the plot second. Choose the library third.
A sophisticated interactive chart cannot rescue the wrong visual encoding. A simple plot can reveal the entire story when it represents the right question.
# Summary - Distribution → histogram, KDE, ECDF, box, violin. - Comparison → bars, box/violin, error bars, facets. - Relationship → scatter, regression, hexbin. - Time → line, rolling trend, uncertainty. - Classification → confusion, ROC, PR, calibration. - Regression → residual diagnostics. - Plotly/Bokeh → browser-native exploration. - Matplotlib/Seaborn → static-first analytical communication and statistical EDA. - Every worked chart in this chapter has independently expandable **data simulator code** and **plot code**, with the visualization left visible. # Learning Resources - Matplotlib: https://matplotlib.org/stable/ - Seaborn: https://seaborn.pydata.org/ - Plotly Python: https://plotly.com/python/ - Bokeh: https://docs.bokeh.org/en/latest/
